subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Kahneman and Tversky's Breakthrough
description: A 60-second lesson on Kahneman and Tversky's Breakthrough.

hook.text: Two psychologists in Jerusalem rewrote economics. They had no economics training. That was the advantage.

buildup.text: Kahneman and Tversky studied how people actually choose under risk, not how models say they should.

discovery.text: Their 1979 paper 'Prospect Theory' became the most cited in all of economics. Written by psychologists.

twist.text: Economists resisted for years. Admitting humans aren't rational agents threatened the entire field's foundation.

climax.text: Kahneman won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002. Tversky had died six years earlier and couldn't share it.

punchline.text: The best economics came from psychology.

quiz.question: What made Kahneman and Tversky's approach different?
options: They studied how people actually decide, not how models predict

details.summary: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published prospect theory in 1979, fundamentally challenging rational choice economics by demonstrating that people evaluate gains and losses relative to reference points, not absolute outcomes.
details.whyItMatters: Prospect theory earned Kahneman the 2002 Nobel Prize and transformed economics. It provided the mathematical framework proving that human decisions are systematically irrational in predictable, measurable ways.
takeaways: Prospect theory was published in Econometrica in 1979
It replaced absolute wealth evaluation with reference-dependent value
Kahneman received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002 for this work

faq.question: Why didn't Tversky share the Nobel Prize?
faq.answer: Amos Tversky died of cancer in 1996, six years before the prize was awarded. Nobel Prizes are not given posthumously. Kahneman has consistently credited Tversky as an equal partner in developing prospect theory.

faq.question: Why was prospect theory so revolutionary?
faq.answer: It provided the first rigorous mathematical alternative to expected utility theory that actually matched observed human behavior. It moved economics from assuming rationality to measuring and modeling systematic irrationality.
